claims.text: Spin-polarized density functional theory can be used to assess whether a material has a ferromagnetic ground state.
Proper treatment of exchange-correlation effects enables spin-polarized DFT to predict a stable ferromagnetic ground state.
The target is a crystalline material, such as a transition-metal alloy, whose magnetic ordering is uncertain.
Total energies of ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, and paramagnetic configurations can be compared using spin-polarized DFT.
The calculations should use a suitable exchange-correlation functional.
Accurate k-point sampling is required for the proposed energy comparison.
An appropriate Hubbard U parameter may be required for correlated systems.
Electronic band structure and localized magnetic moments on metal centers are relevant mediators of magnetic ordering.
Treatment of electron exchange and correlation allows DFT to differentiate the energies of competing magnetic orders.
A ferromagnetic configuration that has the lowest calculated total energy is identified as the predicted ground state under the selected functional.
An energy advantage on the order of tens of meV per atom indicates stable ferromagnetic ordering.
Non-magnetic or antiferromagnetic solutions may be higher in energy than a ferromagnetic solution by a few to tens of meV per atom.
Calculated ferromagnetic stability depends on the exchange-correlation functional, pseudopotentials, and Hubbard U parameter.
DFT magnetic-state predictions can vary with methodological choices and simplifications involving temperature and structural defects.
Experimental verification is needed to establish whether the predicted ferromagnetic ground state occurs.
Observation of an antiferromagnetic or paramagnetic phase instead of a ferromagnetic signal would falsify the proposed magnetic-ground-state prediction.
